newsitem.title: USA: Astronaut Lucid says life now back to normal.
newsitem.headline: Astronaut Lucid says life now back to normal.

text.p: Astronaut Shannon Lucid said on Thursday the effects of her record-breaking stay in space were all but gone and she was savoring some aspects of daily life while settling back into chores such as cleaning and cooking.

A month after her Sept. 26 return from 188 days aboard the Russian space station Mir, Lucid said she had new appreciation for such mundane things as being able to run out to buy a new book or pick up fresh fruit at the grocery store.
"There were a few times (in space) when it really hit you that you were isolated," she told a news conference at Johnson Space Centre.
Now, she said, "I'm living just like I have always lived. I come to work during the day ... then I'm going home and cooking supper and trying to get the house back in shape."
NASA physicians had predicted Lucid would experience weakness and other effects from her six months in weightlessness. But Lucid, 53, said readapting to Earth's gravity had been a breeze.

"Within 24 hours (of return), I was feeling like I was pretty much back to normal," she said. Post-flight tests found, as expected, a slight calcium loss in her bones, but everything else was unchanged, Lucid said.
Lucid's stay on Mir was the longest in space by any U.S. astronaut and a record for a woman.

Lucid praised the Russian cosmonauts with whom she flew and said they never had a disagreement. When not working, they would talk, joke and on weekends watch movies. "Apollo 13," dubbed in Russian, was a favourite.
Lucid said the key to success in a long spaceflight was the chemistry of the crew. "If the people are compatible and get along, then it will be a great flight," she said.
Her initial crewmates were cosmonauts Yuri Onufriyenko and Yuri Usachev. They were replaced in August by Valeri Korzun and Alexander Kaleri.
Lucid said the most memorable moment was a conversation about the Cold War during which she and the two Yuris recalled how they had grown up fearing each other's countries.

"It sort of dawned on all three of us at once how remarkable it was that, here we were, three people who grew up in totally different parts of the world, mortally afraid of each other ... sitting in an outpost in space together, working together and enjoying living together," she said.

Lucid said she had advised designers of the proposed U.S. space station to include a method of getting equipment back to Earth. She said scientific equipment brought to Mir over the years was "stacking up" because there was no way to get it home.
Lucid was replaced on Mir by astronaut John Blaha, who was ferried in aboard the shuttle Atlantis. She admitted she left space with a "certain amount of regret."
"I told John he was going to have a really great time," she said wistfully. Lucid said she would remain in the astronaut corps and hoped to fly in space again.
